A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Neural Low-Discrepancy Sequences, with matching core methods and experiments. All 18 pages of each version, including Appendices A–E, support comparison; the changed formatting does not create material evidence gaps.

before.justification: v1 reports original discrepancy measurements, Borehole integration errors, robot-planning success rates, Black–Scholes prediction errors, and ablation results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds comparator results, architectural comparisons, sampling-efficiency findings, and additional discrepancy analyses.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds an experimental NEUROLDS variant replacing the MLP with a single-layer LSTM. This is a limited architectural adaptation: the recommended MLP, sinusoidal encoding, supervised pretraining, and prefix-discrepancy objective remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Figure 10 introduces one-dimensional sequence evaluation alongside two- and three-dimensional comparisons; v1 already examined the latter dimensions in ablations. The Borehole, four-joint motion-planning, and two-dimensional Black–Scholes tasks remain unchanged. Additional eight-dimensional discrepancy curves reuse dimensional coverage already present in Borehole sampling.

E2.justification: v2 directly evaluates MPMC against NEUROLDS and classical sequences in Figure 1, whereas v1 only discussed MPMC. NMGreedy also joins the Black–Scholes comparison in Table 3 and the discrepancy comparisons in Figures 10–11. These substantially strengthen comparison against learned point-set construction and greedy optimization.

E3.justification: Existing experimental settings are retained, while new comparisons introduce MPMC training at N=1024, independently tuned LSTM/MLP trials at d=4 and N=500, training-length controls at N=1000 versus 5000, and RRT sampling budgets matched by average success. Figure 11 uses weighted star discrepancy with all coordinate weights equal to one; this is additional evaluation, not a documented replacement of the Borehole experiment's sensitivity-weighted symmetric objective.

E4.justification: v2 adds an LSTM-versus-MLP discrepancy/runtime analysis, training-length sensitivity in Figure 12, and matched-success sampling-efficiency analysis for RRT. Figure 1 also directly tests the prefix behavior of a fixed-size MPMC construction. These substantially extend the evidence beyond v1's retained pretraining, AR-GNN, bandwidth, depth, and prefix-weight ablations.

E5.justification: The new LSTM comparison reports average optimization times over five repeated sweeps. The existing 32 Sobol' scramblings and 20 Black–Scholes training runs remain unchanged. No new confidence intervals or significance tests are provided.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2, 5 and 6 and the existing Table 3 scores are retained, but substantial results are added. NMGreedy's Black–Scholes MSE is 4.72×10^-4; MPMC wins at its full target length but generally performs worse on shorter prefixes; and LSTM achieves slightly lower discrepancy with much longer optimization. New RRT findings report that Sobol', Halton and Uniform require respectively 2.50, 1.55 and 2.27 times as many samples to match NEUROLDS's average success. Figures 10–12 add further discrepancy curves.

T1.justification: The mathematical framework, kernels, sequence constructions, and application equations are retained. Equation 2 changes from a square-root expression for discrepancy to an equivalent expression for squared discrepancy. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement now explicitly describe NEUROLDS as generating finite LDS, narrowing the previously unqualified sequence-generation claim. The principal claims concerning discrepancy superiority and usefulness across the three applications remain.

C2.justification: v2 explains MPMC's weaker prefixes through its fixed-size optimization objective and interprets the LSTM result as a small representational benefit outweighed by computational cost. It also qualifies dimensional applicability: improvements are modest in one dimension and clearer in higher dimensions. The existing discussion is otherwise retained.

D1.justification: The added architectural experiment specifies a single-layer LSTM, independent Optuna tuning, best-trial selection, and approximate optimization times of ten minutes for MLP versus over an hour for LSTM. Existing hyperparameters and application details remain unchanged. The same code URL moves from the abstract to Section 3, without a documented access change.

R1.justification: The cited works and central positioning relative to classical QMC and MPMC are retained. The new MPMC experiment supports the existing set-versus-sequence distinction rather than introducing a different relationship to prior work. Bibliographic changes concern formatting and metadata.

P1.justification: v2 adds explanatory paragraphs and an LSTM ablation subsection, introduces a generic Impact Statement, updates affiliations, and relocates the code disclosure. Most prose and the ordering of Sections 1–4 and Appendices A–E remain intact.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column layout to a two-column conference layout. v1's Figures 1–7 are retained as Figures 2–8, with resizing and relocation; five figures are added. Table 3 gains an NMGreedy column, and Table 2 drops its redundant experiment-name column. This substantially changes the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: Direct MPMC and additional NMGreedy comparisons improve empirical support, while the LSTM accuracy–cost analysis better motivates the chosen architecture. Explicitly qualifying generation as finite also improves claim precision. These gains are limited by sparse documentation of some added analyses and unchanged uncertainty reporting for the main results. The new eight-dimensional star-discrepancy plot uses different weights and a different metric from the Borehole experiment, limiting its supporting role.
